definition: Minimalist means deliberately using the fewest and simplest elements possible.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word minimalist. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know minimalist should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The band's minimalist poster — black type on a white field, no image at all — stood out on a wall of screaming color.
Uncluttered is tidy and open, but still full of things — it stops short of minimalist, where the small count itself is the point.
Bare goes further than minimalist: past deliberate restraint into plain emptiness, with nothing chosen at all.

Spare describes the look alone — little is there, and the word says nothing about why. Minimalist adds the philosophy: someone deliberately chose the fewest, simplest elements as a style. A dorm room can be spare because its owner never unpacked; a designer's showroom with one chair is minimalist by conviction.

Pared-down means trimmed back to essentials — something larger was cut away until only what mattered remained. Minimalist names the outlook behind such cutting: fewness chosen on purpose as the style itself. A budget is pared-down out of necessity; a minimalist room is empty of extras by design.

The studio's minimalist watch face shows two hands and twelve dots, nothing else; the designers argued for a year before cutting the date window, because on a face that spare, one more line is a crowd.
Minimalist is precise because the fewness is the design: every element that survived had to justify itself.
A watch face that is merely plain might be cheap or lazy; one pared to two hands on purpose is minimalist.
Minimalist carries intent: someone chose the fewest, simplest elements as a style.
Spare and pared-down describe the look without the philosophy; bare just means empty.
Its true opposite pole in this unit is ornate — the minimalist room and the ornate one disagree about everything except caring how a room looks.

When the new chef took over, the menu shrank from forty dishes to five.
Regulars assumed a struggling kitchen.
The chef assured them the opposite: the short menu was the ambition, not the accident.
Her cooking is minimalist on principle — each plate holds three elements, chosen so that nothing on it can be removed without the dish collapsing.
Critics who expected austerity found precision instead.
One wrote that the five dishes felt larger than the old forty.
Imitators soon learned the hard part: cutting a menu is easy, but choosing the five dishes that deserve to remain is a philosophy.
